Day 75 of 100 · Kubernetes

Kubernetes Services

#100DaysOfCloudAndSecurityKubernetesPublished artifact recovered

A Service gives changing Pods a stable network endpoint and selects its backend endpoints through labels.

Architecture / mental model

client → Service (stable virtual endpoint) → EndpointSlices → matching Ready Pods

How it works

Pods are ephemeral and their IP addresses can change as controllers replace them. A Service lets clients depend on a stable service identity while Kubernetes tracks the matching backend Pods.

The published example selected Pods with `app: web`, listened on Service port 80 and forwarded to container targetPort 8080 as a ClusterIP service.

Service selection is label-driven. The Service object can exist and look perfectly healthy even when its selector matches no Pods, which is why endpoint inspection belongs in troubleshooting.

Hands-on reference

kubectl apply -f service.yaml
kubectl get svc
kubectl describe svc web-service
kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=web-service
kubectl get pods -l app=web --show-labels

Verification

Confirm the Service selector matches the intended Pod labels, inspect EndpointSlices and make a request through the Service from inside the cluster.

Field note / gotcha

A Service selector that matches zero Pods leaves a stable endpoint with nowhere useful to send traffic. Inspect endpoints instead of admiring the Service object.

Security considerations

Choose Service type intentionally. ClusterIP keeps the endpoint cluster-internal by default; NodePort/LoadBalancer change exposure and deserve matching network policy/firewall review.

What I learned

Stable service identity is separated from replaceable workload identity.
